records.title: Sinus rhythm with low voltage in the limb leads
records.explanation: Start with rhythm: look for a P before each QRS and a consistent PR. Then compare QRS amplitudes in the limb leads with the chest leads. The finding being taught is small limb-lead complexes despite an organized sinus rhythm.

records.title: Sinus bradycardia
records.explanation: Use the long strip to count QRS complexes. Look for a regular, slow rhythm with a P before each QRS and a consistent PR. The slow rate is what turns sinus rhythm into sinus bradycardia.

records.title: Normal sinus rhythm
records.explanation: Trace several beats in lead II. Look for a regular rhythm, an upright P before each QRS, and a consistent PR. Those relationships support sinus rhythm.

records.title: Normal sinus rhythm with baseline wander
records.explanation: The baseline drifts gradually. Follow the P-to-QRS relationship across several beats and use the baseline immediately before each beat for comparison. The drift is an artifact clue rather than a rhythm change.

records.title: Inferolateral ST elevation candidate
records.explanation: Compare the J points in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6). Look for a contiguous pattern and check the opposing leads for reciprocal changes. The library labels this an inferolateral ST-elevation candidate.

records.title: Anterior ST elevation candidate
records.explanation: Work across V1–V4 and compare each J point with its own baseline. Look for elevation in neighboring anterior leads and compare the inferior leads for reciprocal depression. This recording is an anterior ST-elevation candidate.

records.title: Inferior and lateral ST elevation candidate
records.explanation: Compare the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with the lateral leads (I, aVL, V5–V6). Ask which contiguous leads show elevation and whether the distribution supports involvement of both territories.

records.title: Anterior and inferior ST elevation candidate
records.explanation: Check the anterior chest leads and the inferior limb leads separately. Compare J points in neighboring leads in each group. This example is labeled as a candidate for ST elevation in both territories.

records.title: Posterior infarct candidate
records.explanation: Inspect V1–V3 for horizontal ST depression and prominent R waves, which can be mirror-image clues to posterior injury. Posterior leads V7–V9 can help clarify the pattern. This case is a posterior infarct candidate.

records.title: S in I, Q in III
records.explanation: Compare QRS shapes in I and III: the finding to look for is an S wave in I and a Q wave in III. Check the T wave in III separately. These findings alone cannot establish a cause.

records.title: Possible RV strain comparison
records.explanation: Compare V1–V4 and the inferior leads for repolarization changes. Check rightward axis or right bundle morphology as additional clues. The tracing is a comparison case for possible RV strain, which has several causes.

records.title: VT candidate with conflicting label
records.explanation: Start with QRS width, regularity and the relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats support VT. This recording has conflicting labels, so it is best used to compare possibilities.

records.title: VT candidate
records.explanation: Assess the regularity and width of the tachycardia. Search across leads for P waves marching independently or for capture and fusion beats, which support ventricular origin. The source labels this a VT candidate.

records.title: Wide-complex tachycardia comparison
records.explanation: Compare QRS shape across the chest leads and look for independent atrial activity. A wide, fast rhythm can reflect VT or a supraventricular rhythm with aberrancy or pre-excitation. Width alone cannot distinguish them.

records.title: Complete AV block candidate
records.explanation: March out the P waves and QRS complexes separately. The finding to verify is that both march independently, with the apparent PR interval changing and no consistent conduction between them. Compare lead II and V1 if P waves are hard to see.

records.title: Wenckebach candidate
records.explanation: Find a sequence of conducted beats around a dropped QRS. Progressive PR lengthening before the dropped beat, followed by a shorter PR when conduction resumes, is the Wenckebach pattern.

records.title: SVT candidate
records.explanation: Check whether the tachycardia is regular and narrow, then search for atrial activity in II and V1. P waves may be buried in the QRS or appear just after it. The library labels this an SVT candidate.

records.title: Precordial ST depression
records.explanation: Focus on the chest leads and compare the J point and early ST segment with the local baseline. Look for horizontal or downsloping depression in contiguous leads. The ST finding alone does not establish its cause.

records.title: Subtle lateral ST depression
records.explanation: Compare I, aVL, V5 and V6 against their own baselines. Pay attention to subtle horizontal or downsloping ST segments across neighboring lateral leads. A repeated change is more useful than one noisy beat.

records.title: Atrial fibrillation
records.explanation: Compare several R–R intervals on the long strip. Irregularly irregular spacing with no consistent P waves supports atrial fibrillation. Zoom in on V1 or II if atrial activity is subtle.

records.title: Atrial fibrillation with RVR
records.explanation: Use the long strip to check for irregularly irregular R–R intervals without consistent P waves, then count the ventricular rate manually. The rapid ventricular response refers to the QRS rate. Compare it with the automated estimate.

records.title: Atrial flutter with slow response
records.explanation: Inspect II, III, aVF and V1 between QRS complexes for repeating flutter waves. Compare the fast atrial activity with the slower ventricular response to identify how many atrial waves occur per QRS.

records.title: Right bundle branch block
records.explanation: Compare V1 with I and V6. A terminal positive deflection in V1 and a broad terminal S wave in the lateral leads support right bundle branch block. Check QRS duration to assess whether the block is complete.

records.title: Left bundle branch block
records.explanation: Compare the deep negative QRS in V1 with the broad or notched lateral R wave in I, aVL, V5 or V6. That combination with a wide QRS supports left bundle branch block.

records.title: First-degree AV block
records.explanation: Measure from P onset to QRS onset over several beats. A consistently prolonged PR interval above 200 ms with every P wave followed by a QRS supports first-degree AV block.

records.title: Inferior ST elevation candidate
records.explanation: Compare the J point in II, III and aVF and look for reciprocal depression in I or aVL. This is an inferior ST-elevation candidate, so assess the full pattern across contiguous leads.

records.title: Anterior ST elevation candidate
records.explanation: Work across V1–V4 and compare each J point with its own baseline. Look for elevation in neighboring anterior leads and compare the inferior leads for reciprocal depression. This recording is an anterior ST-elevation candidate.

records.title: Sinus rhythm with a PVC
records.explanation: Find the beat that arrives early and has a wider, different QRS shape. Compare it with the surrounding sinus beats and look for a preceding P wave and a pause afterward. Those clues help identify a PVC.

records.title: Ventricular bigeminy
records.explanation: Follow the repeating sequence across the long strip. A sinus beat alternating with an early ventricular beat produces ventricular bigeminy.

records.title: Ventricular trigeminy
records.explanation: Follow the repeating sequence across the long strip. Two conducted beats followed by an early ventricular beat produce ventricular trigeminy.

records.title: Acute anteroseptal MI with ST elevation · A07802
records.explanation: Compare V1–V3, particularly V2 and V3, for J-point elevation and abnormal early QRS forces. The source labels this acute anteroseptal MI with ST elevation. Compare contiguous leads and the baseline before each beat.

records.title: ST depression · A02868
records.explanation: Compare the ST segment to the preceding isoelectric baseline in neighboring leads. Look for persistent horizontal or downsloping depression across beats. The tracing demonstrates a repolarization finding whose cause depends on context.

records.title: Early repolarization · A10453
records.explanation: Inspect the end of the QRS for a small notch or slur at the J point and see how the ST segment rises afterward. Compare adjacent leads and consider the distribution and any reciprocal changes before attributing ST elevation to early repolarization.

records.title: LVH with strain · A13780
records.explanation: Compare QRS voltage and polarity with the ST–T changes. In LVH with strain, tall lateral R waves may be accompanied by downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T-wave inversion. Check I, aVL, V5 and V6 first.

records.title: LVH with strain · A20682
records.explanation: Compare QRS voltage and polarity with the ST–T changes. In LVH with strain, tall lateral R waves may be accompanied by downsloping ST depression and asymmetric T-wave inversion. Check I, aVL, V5 and V6 first.

records.title: Mobitz II · A09204
records.explanation: Find P waves that arrive on time. Look for an occasional P wave without a following QRS while the PR stays similar on conducted beats. That pattern favors Mobitz II over progressive PR lengthening.

records.title: Mobitz II · A25353
records.explanation: Compare PR intervals before each dropped QRS. The source includes both Mobitz I and Mobitz II labels. Progressive PR lengthening favors Wenckebach, while a similar PR on conducted beats favors Mobitz II. Use this as a comparison tracing.

records.explanation: Look between QRS complexes in II, III, aVF and V1 for repeated atrial deflections with a consistent cycle length. Compare the atrial and ventricular rates. Flutter can have fixed or variable AV conduction.

records.title: Ventricular preexcitation · A09221
records.explanation: In the long lead I strip, look for the subtle slurred foot just before the steep R wave. Early activation through an accessory pathway can cause this delta-like onset. PR and QRS duration are unavailable, so this is a subtle source-labeled case. Counting the visible QRS complexes gives a rate in the 70s, which disagrees with the automated estimate.

records.title: Ventricular preexcitation · A19062
records.explanation: Check for a slurred QRS onset across leads. This recording’s estimates show a short PR (96 ms) and wide QRS (188 ms), both supportive of pre-excitation when paired with a delta wave.

records.title: Ventricular preexcitation · A24957
records.explanation: Compare QRS onset across several leads and look for a slurred initial deflection close to the P wave. This is source-labeled ventricular pre-excitation. Without reliable automated intervals, use the grid to check PR and QRS width directly.
